doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

title: What bothers him: showboating and bandstand competition
summary: He dislikes playing for sport and 'battle of the bones' atmospheres.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: You strike me as a fairly even-keeled guy. I wonder if there’s anything that really gets on your nerves musically.

I’m not one for showboating or one-upmanship on the bandstand, you know, people that play for sport, that it’s more like a competition than a sharing kind of a thing. My favorite players are the guys that, even on like instruments — my favorite trombone players to play with are the guys where you play something and the other guy doesn’t feel obligated to play it back better or higher or faster. And there are a lot of cases of people doing that, where you don’t really feel like you’re making music together, it’s just like — for lack of a better term, excuse my French, but a pissing contest, you know? And I get to the point where that really turns me off. And I actually just kind of revert to staying out of the game. So you’ve got one guy who’s all over the place, and one guy just okay let’s calm down here. And it doesn’t make for a good program, but I can’t live in that room. That’s kind of not my personality. I found out a long time ago that’s not my personality. So that’s the only thing. It doesn’t make me mad, it’s just disappointing because you want to make music and you get in those situations and it’s like oh — and that is the mentality in a lot of those festival type atmospheres. They want to hear everybody pitted against everybody and the battle of the bones, or things like — you know, but it’s much more fun to me when it’s just like playing music. You do your thing, I do my thing and let’s just kind of make it work like you would if you were talking to somebody.
